text: New Jersey's minimum wage rose from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour on April 1, 1992; Card and Krueger surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania before (February-March 1992) and after (November-December 1992) the rise.

Card and Krueger define full-time-equivalent employment as the number of full-time workers, including managers and assistant managers, plus 0.5 times the number of part-time workers (p. 775; Table 5 notes).
In Card and Krueger's Table 3, wave-2 employment is set to zero at the six permanently closed stores and treated as missing at the four temporarily closed stores.
Card and Krueger (1994, Table 3, row 3) report a difference-in-differences of 2.76 FTE employees per store (standard error 1.36; t = 2.03), about 13 percent, in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania.

In the balanced sample of stores with employment data in both waves, the published difference-in-differences is 2.75 (standard error 1.34) (Card and Krueger 1994, Table 3, row 4); setting the temporarily closed stores to zero gives 2.51 (1.35) (row 5).
Mean FTE employment per store fell from 23.33 to 21.17 in Pennsylvania and rose from 20.44 to 21.03 in New Jersey (Card and Krueger 1994, Table 3, rows 1-2).

On 357 stores with employment and starting-wage data in both waves, the New Jersey coefficient in a regression of the change in FTE employment is 2.33 (1.19) without controls and 2.30 (1.20) with chain and ownership controls (Card and Krueger 1994, Table 4).
Within New Jersey, the change in FTE employment at stores initially paying $4.25 exceeded that at stores paying $5.00 or more by 3.36 (1.48) (Card and Krueger 1994, Table 3, column vii).

Using payroll records from fast-food restaurants in the same area, Neumark and Wascher estimate that the New Jersey increase reduced employment by 4.6 percent relative to Pennsylvania, an elasticity of -0.24, and report that the standard deviation of employment change in Card and Krueger's survey data is about three times that in the payroll data.
Excluding closed stores and controlling for chain and ownership, Neumark and Wascher obtain a difference-in-differences of 2.78 FTE on Card and Krueger's survey data.

Using BLS ES-202 payroll records, Card and Krueger find similar or slightly faster fast-food employment growth in New Jersey than in eastern Pennsylvania after the 1992 increase, and attribute the Neumark-Wascher result to the Pennsylvania restaurants of a single franchisee and to differences in reporting intervals.
With a small number of policy changes, conventional difference-in-differences inference can be misleading, and the treatment-effect estimator should not be treated as consistent.
The public archive njmin.zip contains public.dat (410 observations), a codebook, a SAS program for key tabulations, and the texts of both survey waves.
An earlier informal replication from the public data reproduces the Table 3 means and a difference-in-differences of 2.75, but not the published standard errors or the 357-store regression sample.

Using changes-in-changes on the original Card and Krueger data, on 301 New Jersey and 75 Pennsylvania stores (eight New Jersey stores outside the Pennsylvania support dropped), Ropponen reports an average effect of 0.90 FTE (bootstrap SE 0.44), against a difference-in-differences of 2.72 on the same 376 stores, which he says corresponds to Card and Krueger's 2.75; effects are positive for small and negative for large restaurants.
Applying changes-in-changes to both the Card-Krueger and Neumark-Wascher data, Ropponen (2011) concludes that the positive employment result holds only for small fast-food restaurants.
Re-estimating both studies with Abadie's semiparametric difference-in-differences, Ropponen (2014) finds the original overall employment effects fairly robust.

Neumark and Wascher state that the greater variability of employment changes in Card and Krueger's data is not driven by one or two outliers; the standard deviation of employment change is 9.6 in the survey data against 3.2 in the payroll data.
A 2025 preprint replication reports a difference-in-differences of 3.36 (SE about 1.68) and a balanced-sample estimate of 3.44, not the published 2.76 and 2.75.

Replicated Table 3 row 3 difference-in-differences: change in mean FTE employment per store, New Jersey minus Pennsylvania, February-March to November-December 1992 (FTE employees per store; unbalanced sample, all stores with employment data in each wave). Row 3 is reproduced within the pre-registered 0.05 tolerance but not at published precision: the replicated row 3 prints 2.75 / -2.17 / 0.59 (DiD / PA / NJ) against the published 2.76 / -2.16 / 0.59; the published entries imply an unrounded NJ change in (0.590, 0.595) and PA change in (-2.165, -2.160), and the replicated 0.5880 and -2.1656 lie outside, so the gap is not rounding and its source is unidentified (data vintage or an inconsistency in the published table are possible). The gap is in the unbalanced wave means: rows 1-3 use the same wave samples and the replicated row 3 is exactly row 2 minus row 1, so the published row 3 implies unrounded wave means that differ from the replicated ones below the printed precision; rows 1-2 match only at their two printed decimals, while the balanced row 4, row 5, and the Table 4 coefficient, SE, N, root MSE and SD match (the Table 4 dependent mean, -0.2375 vs published -0.237, is just outside rounding). Whether the difference lies among the 26 stores observed in one wave only (PA 2+2, NJ 12+10) or is a sub-rounding data difference is a conjecture.
